title: Festivals & events
headline: A year of feast days, races and masks
tagline: Bareback horse races, orange battles, flower carpets and candlelit processions: plan your trip around one of Italy's great festivals and you will never forget it.

hero_image.alt: Racehorses' hooves pounding the packed earth of Piazza del Campo during the Palio di Siena
hero_image.credit: Roberto Vicario, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

intro: Italian festivals are not put on for visitors. Most are centuries-old rituals of rivalry and devotion, run by neighbourhoods, guilds and confraternities who rehearse all year. In Siena, people are baptised into their contrada; in Gubbio, the men who carry the Ceri train like athletes; in Catania, hundreds of thousands follow the relics of St Agatha through the night. Watching, you are a guest at someone else's party.

That makes them unforgettable, and a little chaotic. Hotels fill months ahead, streets close and timetables slip. Below is a month-by-month calendar of the big ones, the headline events worth building a trip around, and the arts and food fairs that fill the gaps. Many dates follow Easter or the saints' calendar, so always check the year's programme before you book.

sections.heading: The festival calendar, month by month
sections.intro: Fixed dates repeat every year; moveable ones are tied to Easter, Carnival or a weekend, so confirm locally.

items.title: Sant'Antonio Abate and the Mamuthones
items.subtitle: Mamoiada, Sardinia
items.desc: Bonfires burn across inland Sardinia, and in Mamoiada the Mamuthones make their first outing of the year: men in black sheepskins and dark wooden masks, shaking heavy cowbells in a slow, eerie march.

items.title: Festa di Sant'Agata
items.subtitle: Catania, Sicily
items.desc: One of the largest religious festivals in the world. Devotees in white robes haul the saint's silver carriage through the city for two days and nights, with fireworks, giant candles and torrone stalls.

items.title: Carnevale di Venezia
items.subtitle: Venice, Veneto
items.desc: Masks, costumed balls and the Flight of the Angel from the Campanile in St Mark's Square. The best moments are early morning, when costumed Venetians pose in empty campi. In 2027 it ends on 9 February.

items.title: Carnevale di Viareggio
items.subtitle: Viareggio, Tuscany
items.desc: Giant papier-mache floats, some as tall as a building, satirise politicians and celebrities as they roll along the seafront promenade over several weekends.

items.title: Battle of the Oranges
items.subtitle: Ivrea, Piedmont
items.desc: For three days, teams on foot pelt armoured carts with oranges in a mock revolt against a medieval tyrant. Spectators who wear the red Phrygian cap are off-limits; everyone else is fair game.

items.title: Processione dei Misteri
items.subtitle: Trapani, Sicily
items.desc: Twenty groups of carved wooden statues of the Passion are carried through the old town, swaying to brass bands, for around 24 hours from Good Friday afternoon.

items.title: Scoppio del Carro
items.subtitle: Florence, Tuscany
items.desc: An ornate cart packed with fireworks is pulled by white oxen to the Duomo; at the Gloria, a dove-shaped rocket shoots down a wire from the altar and sets it off in a roar of smoke and bangs.

items.title: Corsa dei Ceri
items.subtitle: Gubbio, Umbria
items.desc: Three wooden towers topped by saints, each around 280 kg, are raced through the streets and up Monte Ingino at full tilt by teams of bearers in coloured shirts.

items.title: Infiorata di Noto
items.subtitle: Noto, Sicily
items.desc: Via Nicolaci is carpeted in pictures made from flower petals, framed by Baroque balconies. Spello in Umbria and Genzano near Rome hold their own spectacular infiorate for Corpus Domini in late spring.

items.title: La Biennale di Venezia
items.subtitle: Venice, Veneto
items.desc: The world's most famous contemporary art show alternates yearly with the Architecture Biennale, spreading through the Giardini, the Arsenale and palazzi across the city.

items.title: Calcio Storico Fiorentino
items.subtitle: Florence, Tuscany
items.desc: Part rugby, part wrestling, in 16th-century costume on a sand pitch in Piazza Santa Croce. Four neighbourhoods fight it out, with the final on 24 June, the feast of St John.

items.title: Palio di Siena
items.subtitle: Siena, Tuscany
items.desc: Ten horses, bareback riders and three laps of the Campo in about 90 seconds. The days before are full of trial races, blessings of the horses in church and long outdoor contrada dinners.

items.title: Festino di Santa Rosalia
items.subtitle: Palermo, Sicily
items.desc: A towering triumphal cart carries Palermo's patron saint, who saved the city from plague in 1624, down the Cassaro to the sea, followed by fireworks over the Foro Italico.

items.title: Festa del Redentore
items.subtitle: Venice, Veneto
items.desc: Venetians tie their boats together in the Bacino di San Marco, eat dinner on the water and watch a huge fireworks display. On Sunday a bridge of boats links the Zattere with Palladio's Redentore church.

items.title: La Notte della Taranta
items.subtitle: Melpignano, Puglia
items.desc: The summer-long pizzica festival in Salento's villages ends with a free all-night concert for tens of thousands in Melpignano.

items.title: Venice International Film Festival
items.subtitle: Lido di Venezia, Veneto
items.desc: The oldest film festival in the world, on the Lido. Public tickets are sold for many screenings, and stars arrive by water taxi along the red carpet.

items.title: Regata Storica
items.subtitle: Venice, Veneto
items.desc: A water parade of 16th-century-style boats and costumed gondoliers, followed by fierce rowing races down the Grand Canal.

items.title: Macchina di Santa Rosa
items.subtitle: Viterbo, Lazio
items.desc: A 30-metre illuminated tower is carried on the shoulders of about a hundred facchini through the dark medieval streets, with the lights turned off around them.

items.title: Barcolana
items.subtitle: Trieste, Friuli-Venezia Giulia
items.desc: Probably the most crowded sailing regatta on the planet, with often more than 1,800 boats jostling on one start line in the Gulf of Trieste, with a week of parties along the waterfront.

items.title: Alba White Truffle Fair
items.subtitle: Alba, Piedmont
items.desc: Weekends of truffle market, tastings and cooking shows, plus a donkey palio. The 2026 edition, the 96th, runs from 10 October to 6 December.

items.title: Lucca Comics & Games
items.subtitle: Lucca, Tuscany
items.desc: Europe's biggest comics and gaming festival takes over the walled city, with cosplayers queuing for pastries under Renaissance ramparts.

items.title: Autumnia
items.subtitle: Figline e Incisa Valdarno, Tuscany
items.desc: A free farming, food and environment fair between Chianti and the Pratomagno: a market of local producers, a farmyard of piglets and calves, and guided visits to the Teatro Garibaldi and Palazzo Pretorio. The 2026 edition runs 6-8 November.

items.title: Festa della Salute
items.subtitle: Venice, Veneto
items.desc: A temporary bridge of boats crosses the Grand Canal to the domed Salute church, built to give thanks for the end of the 1630 plague. Venetians light candles and eat castradina, a smoked mutton stew.

items.title: Prima della Scala
items.subtitle: Milan, Lombardy
items.desc: La Scala's season opens on the feast of Sant'Ambrogio with a black-tie gala, while the Oh Bej! Oh Bej! street fair runs around the Castello Sforzesco.

items.title: Christmas markets of Alto Adige
items.subtitle: Bolzano, Merano, Bressanone, Brunico, Vipiteno
items.desc: Wooden huts, mulled wine, Zelten fruit bread and handmade decorations in the Alpine towns of South Tyrol, with snowy peaks behind.

sections.heading: Six festivals worth building a trip around

items.title: Palio di Siena
items.subtitle: Siena, 2 July and 16 August
items.desc: Not a show but the climax of a year of passion for Siena's seventeen contrade. Stand in the centre of the Campo for free (arrive hours early, with water) or pay for a balcony seat. Don't miss the historical parade before the race.

image.alt: Armoured figures and the ox-drawn carroccio in the historical parade before the Palio di Siena
image.credit: William Domenichini, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

items.title: Carnevale di Venezia
items.subtitle: Venice, before Lent
items.desc: Rent a costume or simply buy a handmade mask from a workshop, not a stall. The first weekend has the Festa Veneziana on the water; the final days bring the crowds. Midweek and early mornings are magical.

image.alt: Two masked revellers in feathered costumes at the Carnival of Venice
image.credit: Frank Kovalchek, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

items.title: Battle of the Oranges
items.subtitle: Ivrea, Carnival
items.desc: The messiest festival in Italy: tonnes of oranges flying through the air in the town's squares. Watch from behind the nets or buy a red cap to stay out of the fight. Wear old clothes either way.

image.alt: Helmeted orange-throwers on a cart under a shower of oranges at the Ivrea Carnival
image.credit: Baldo Simone, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

items.title: Corsa dei Ceri
items.subtitle: Gubbio, 15 May
items.desc: From dawn the town is a sea of yellow, blue and black shirts. The Ceri are raised in Piazza Grande at midday and paraded all afternoon, then raced at full tilt through the streets and up the mountain to the basilica of St Ubaldo in the early evening.

image.alt: Ceraioli in yellow shirts straining under the poles of a Cero during the Corsa dei Ceri in Gubbio
image.credit: Louis Gino Borsella, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

items.title: Regata Storica
items.subtitle: Venice, first Sunday of September
items.desc: The Grand Canal at its most glorious: gilded ceremonial boats, rowers in Renaissance costume and the gondolino races cheered from every palazzo window. Book a canal-side table or join the crowds on the Rialto.

image.alt: The white Baroque facade of Ca' Rezzonico on the Grand Canal, along the Regata Storica course
image.credit: Didier Descouens, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

items.title: Christmas in South Tyrol
items.subtitle: Late November to early January
items.desc: Bolzano's market fills Piazza Walther with wooden chalets; Merano's runs along the river promenade; Bressanone's sits beneath the cathedral. Ride the cable car to Renon for snowy views and an early dinner of dumplings.

image.alt: A wooden Christmas market stall glowing with lights and decorations in Bolzano
image.credit: Skafa, CC BY-SA 2.5, via Wikimedia Commons

sections.heading: Arts, film and food fairs
sections.intro: Big cultural events that bring a city to life for weeks, not days.

items.title: Biennale Arte
items.subtitle: Venice
items.desc: The 2026 edition, the 61st, runs from 9 May to 22 November. Architecture takes over in odd-numbered years, with dance, theatre and music festivals in between.

items.title: Venice Film Festival
items.subtitle: Lido di Venezia
items.desc: The 2026 festival ran 2-12 September. Tickets for public screenings go on sale in August.

items.title: Festival dei Due Mondi
items.subtitle: Spoleto, Umbria
items.desc: Founded in 1958, this festival of opera, theatre, dance and music fills the hill town's theatres and squares from late June into July.

items.title: Umbria Jazz
items.subtitle: Perugia, Umbria
items.desc: Ten days of jazz in July with free stages in the medieval squares, plus a winter edition in Orvieto at New Year.

items.title: Sagre
items.subtitle: Everywhere, all summer and autumn
items.desc: Village food festivals devoted to one dish or ingredient, from chestnuts to wild boar to fried fish, with long tables, local wine and a dance band. Look for posters on the roadside.

tips: Book accommodation as soon as you have dates: Siena in early July, Venice at Carnival and Gubbio on 15 May fill up months ahead.
Many moveable feasts depend on Easter; in 2027 Easter Sunday falls on 28 March, with Carnival ending on 9 February.
At crowded events, agree on a meeting point, keep bags small and drink plenty of water; you may not be able to leave the Campo during the Palio.
Patron saints' days often mean shops and offices close in that town; check before planning museum visits.
Respect the ritual: festivals like the Palio and Sant'Agata are deeply serious to locals, so don't push into processions for photos.
